draft.title: Recurrence relations in Specialist
card: A recurrence relation gives each term using earlier terms. You also need starting values to get the sequence going.
A first-order relation uses only the previous term, such as t(n+1) = 2 × t(n). It needs one starting value.
A second-order relation uses the two previous terms, such as t(n+2) = t(n+1) + t(n). It needs two starting values.
The Fibonacci sequence has t1 = 1, t2 = 1 and t(n+2) = t(n+1) + t(n), giving 1, 1, 2, 3, 5, 8. Terms can also be multiplied first, such as t(n+2) = 3 × t(n+1) − t(n).
draft.remember: Start with the given values, then build each new term from the earlier ones, one step at a time.

a.q: A sequence has t1 = 1, t2 = 3 and t(n+2) = t(n+1) + t(n). What is t6?
a.why: The terms are 1, 3, 4, 7, 11, 18, so t6 = 18. The value 11 is t5, which comes from stopping one term too soon.
a.clue: Write out each term in order, adding the previous two.

b.q: A sequence has t1 = 1, t2 = 2 and t(n+2) = 2 × t(n+1) + t(n). What is t5?
b.why: t3 = 2 × 2 + 1 = 5, t4 = 2 × 5 + 2 = 12 and t5 = 2 × 12 + 5 = 29. The value 12 is t4, and 8 comes from ignoring the 2 and adding the previous two terms.
b.clue: The 2 multiplies the term just before, not the one before that.

problems.detail: "Terms can also be multiplied first" is ambiguous. It could be read as multiplying terms by each other, when it means multiplying a term by a constant, as in 3 × t(n+1). Something like "Earlier terms can also be multiplied by a number" would be clearer.

check.summary: Both answers check out: t6 = 18 and t5 = 29, and the explanations are correct. The only issue is one ambiguous phrase in the card about multiplying terms.
